html:
The Dyirbal, or Jirrbal, are an Aboriginal Australian people of the rainforest of north Queensland, on the upper Tully River and the southern Atherton Tableland. The map shows them from 1600 to 1800.

The name covers one tribe, the Dyirbalngan, and also a set of related neighbouring peoples, among them the Yidinji, the Mbabaram and the Warrgamay. Rainforest life here was unusual in Australia: people processed toxic nuts and seeds by slicing, soaking and roasting them to make them safe.

Their language is famous among linguists. The linguist R. M. W. Dixon studied it from the 1960s. Dyirbal sorts its nouns into four classes, one of which groups women, fire and dangerous things, which gave the title to a well-known 1987 book by George Lakoff. It also had a special "mother-in-law" speech style, used in the presence of certain relatives. See Aboriginal Australian societies.
